speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: asked the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (a) what are the average waiting times at polyclinics for walk-in patients during peak and off-peak hours; and (b) whether there are plans to redistribute patient load across off-peak hours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: That is why it is important for us to operate on an appointment basis as much as possible, to optimise capacity and patient waiting times and to spread out patient arrivals across the day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: That said, we always schedule fewer appointments than full capacity to accommodate walk-in patients with acute medical needs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it is an improvement from the last time this question was asked two years ago, which was 17 minutes and 164 minutes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But a one-and-a half-hour waiting time is still quite long.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am wondering whether there are any plans to maybe introduce more capacity for polyclinics.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think that is a question that many patients also ask.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because in the midst of increasing capacity, we also want to optimise the use of that capacity.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We could actually leave a lot of empty slots just in case there are walk-in patients, but that means there will be a lot of time wasted that will not be used if there are no walk-in patients.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In the sense, there will always be a trade-off there.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: When we do schedule appointments, we hope that we can stick to the time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: When the patient arrives, we then serve the patient within that allocated time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But as you can imagine, it is often not so straightforward to determine ahead of time how that conversation and the consultation with each particular patient will go.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Even if we allocate, say, 15 minutes for what we think is a reasonable consultation time, sometimes the patient that comes in that time slot may have a very complex issue or multiple medical problems that takes a far longer conversation and examination to complete.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In which case, it may take half an hour and, therefore, it eats into the next patient's consultation time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In a busy clinic, sometimes, such long conversations, on a particular day, you may have quite a few complicated patients that come in sequentially.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That means that there will, therefore, be a snowball effect and patients who are seen at the later part of the session, of the morning session or afternoon session, will therefore end up experiencing a longer waiting time, even though they have been given a scheduled appointment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, there are quite a lot of complicated dynamics happening in a clinic on a day-to-day basis and it is very hard to predict ahead of time how each day will pan out.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Again, like I said, if you are towards the end of that morning session where the prior patients before you had longer conversations, that snowballs into a much longer waiting time for those at the end of that session.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is what a healthcare clinic usually goes through and we will try our very best to resource with more consultation slots to actually meet all those demands.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: What the clinic tries to do is that, for those who turn up in a walk-in manner and for which the staff triage that this is actually not something that is an emergency or extremely urgent, they will try to schedule the next day's appointment for this resident, so that he or she can come back the following day without having to be subjected to a long waiting time as a sudden walk-in patient.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I hope that kind of gives the Member a sense of how complicated it is, but how the efforts are still being made to try and reduce waiting time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am empathetic to the arguments of efficiency and ensuring that patients can see a polyclinic doctor or consultation as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand the Senior Minister of State mentioned it is important to try and make a make an appointment so that your waiting time is within a certain period.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But can I ask the Senior of Minister, is the Ministry taking note of how many people are actually walking in vis-a-vis making scheduled appointments?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I ask this in the context of a super aged society, because there is also the added problem of difficulty in making appointments for certain individuals, especially those who live alone, for example.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I think, in general, most patients who do not have pressing issues will try to fix an appointment because they want certainty of time and to also reduce their waiting time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The Clerk will proceed to read the Orders of the Day.

speaker: The Chairman
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), provided that Members had not asked for questions standing in their names to be postponed to a later Sitting day or withdrawn, written answers to questions not reached by the end of Question Time are reproduced in the Appendix.]
